items.title: Akiyoshi Toshiko — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: my first recording, which was done by Norman Granz

ctx.x: And Bud Powell‟s record was … the first one, I think he was 23 years old, his first [as a] leader. And my first recording, which was done by Norman Granz, you know, at the recommendation from the late Oscar Peterson, I was 23 years old, so I thought, “Whoa, this is something!” [laughs]
[Laughs] Let‟s go back to when you first got to Tokyo, um, about your impressions of Tokyo, and where you first stayed. Did you have any con … you had this letter of introduction,

items.title: Toshiko Akiyoshi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 17, 1999
items.q: so after I had this chance making records for Norman Granz which was in ’53

ctx.x: No, nothing. So you learn that way. And there’s another very precious lesson in those days, were drafted musicians from here, professional ones, some of them noteworthy like Hampton Hawes for example that’s a noted player. Even those not that noted, Eddie Costa. There was a drum player, later he was playing with Eddie’s group or somebody like that. But anyway, there were quite many good players in Japan in the Army and, not Navy, but Air Force band. And they would come and sit in where I had my own group. And I…
Did you start writing them down, or did they just become memorized immediately yourself?
